news.headline: TRAI mandates AI-led complaint centres, 16-hour human support
news.story_lead: TRAI mandates AI-led complaint centres, 16-hour human support TRAI mandates 24/7 AI-enabled complaint centres, human support for 16 hours daily, faster appeals and penalties up to ₹ 20 lakh for mishandled cases. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has directed telecom operators and internet service providers (ISPs) to run round-the-clock complaint centres that can be handled by AI agents, while mandating human assistance for at least 16 hours a day. It has also introduced penalties of up to ₹ 20 lakh per quarter per service area for improper disposal or handling of consumer disputes, under amended telecom consumer complaint redressal rules released on Monday.
news.full_article_text: TRAI mandates AI-led complaint centres, 16-hour human support TRAI mandates 24/7 AI-enabled complaint centres, human support for 16 hours daily, faster appeals and penalties up to ₹ 20 lakh for mishandled cases. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has directed telecom operators and internet service providers (ISPs) to run round-the-clock complaint centres that can be handled by AI agents, while mandating human assistance for at least 16 hours a day. It has also introduced penalties of up to ₹ 20 lakh per quarter per service area for improper disposal or handling of consumer disputes, under amended telecom consumer complaint redressal rules released on Monday. TRAI said the rules would be published in the gazette. For the first time, the telecom regulator has included AI-based customer care services in a binding rule under the Telecom Consumer Complaint Redressal (Fourth Amendment) Regulations, 2026. The rules, amended after more than a decade, were last revised on July 1, 2014. The amended regulation 3(3) requires AI systems to “operate with appropriate human oversight” and consumers to receive “a notification” that they are speaking to an AI agent. Under the amended rules, service providers will be charged ₹ 1,000 for every complaint and ₹ 5,000 for every appeal found to have been wrongly disposed of, with penalties capped at ₹ 20 lakh per quarter per service area. TRAI also directed operators to submit quarterly performance reports, including number of complaints and appeals received, disposed of and pending, time taken for disposal and feedback survey results, in a format specified by the regulator. Late submission of quarterly reports will attract penalties of up to ₹ 5,000 a day for 15 days and ₹ 20,000 a day thereafter, capped at ₹ 10 lakh per licensed service area. The draft regulations were released on May 7, with stakeholder comments invited until June 12 and countercomments until June 19. TRAI received 32 comments and 24 countercomments, which it uploaded to its website. An open house discussion was held on July 17. Operators opposed the 24x7 complaint-centre requirement on cost grounds. In its explanatory memorandum, TRAI said some stakeholders objected to round-the-clock operations, “citing disproportionate costs and limited benefit”. The regulator responded that the requirement “does not necessarily imply deployment of the same level of resources 24x7”. TRAI received 73,081 complaints in 2025-26, up from 44,733 in 2023-24, pointing to dissatisfaction with operators’ grievance redressal systems. Some stakeholders have also questioned whether TRAI can impose penalties through regulations. The penalties under the current rule are new, however the regulator has been imposing financial disincentives under the Standards of Quality of Service of Access (Wireline and Wireless) and Broadband (Wireline and Wireless) Service Regulations, 2024. This was also a concern for some stakeholders who said this may result in double penalties on telecom service providers. But TRAI said the two serve “distinct regulatory objectives”. The telecom regulator has also scrapped the advisory committees and replaced them with oversight committees in every service provider to oversee and periodically review the functioning of its grievance redressal mechanism. Consumer groups, who sent 22 of the 32 comments on the draft, opposed the move, with one saying it makes the system “operator reviewing operator”. TRAI said the committees caused delays, making the appellate process inadequate. Appeal timelines have also been halved, with consumers getting 15 days instead of 30 to appeal and the appellate authority is required to decide within 15 days. Helplines must use a standard IVRS menu with separate options for complaints, appeals and queries, along with a human option and a call-back facility. Complaints can be registered through apps and websites, with status updates by SMS and email, and service must be offered in a state official language besides Hindi and English. After every closed complaint, consumers will be asked to rate the resolution from 1 to 5, and the results will be published quarterly. Disputes must be resolved through a non-chargeable numbers instead of a dedicated toll-free system, providers must set up dedicated desks and accessible apps for persons with disabilities, and records must be kept for six months, up from three. ISPs with 10,000 or fewer subscribers are exempt from the rules, which consumer groups said leaves small-town and rural users without a remedy. Satellite service providers are also covered under the rules, while OTT services are outside TRAI’s jurisdiction. The rules take effect 30 days after Gazette publication. The oversight committee, survey and reporting rules apply after 60 days, and the 24x7 centres, IVRS and app rules after 90 days. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Sejal Sharma I am a technology policy reporter with the National Political Bureau at Hindustan Times, based in New Delhi. I cover digital policy and the intersection of technology and society, focusing mainly on what's happening in India. My beat often involves tracking platform regulation, privacy, internet curbs, and the real-world impact of digital rules, among other things. TRAI also directed operators to submit quarterly performance reports, including number of complaints and appeals received, disposed of and pending, time taken for disposal and feedback survey results, in a format specified by the regulator.

news.full_article_text: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall in Andhra Pradesh, triggers heavy rain; thousands evacuated, coastal areas on alert Andhra Pradesh had stepped up evacuation and disaster management measures ahead of the cyclone's arrival. Severe cyclonic storm Murasu made landfall along the south Andhra Pradesh coast early Tuesday, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds to the region. The storm crossed the coastline near Ongole in Prakasam district at around 1am, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). Track live updates The cyclone made landfall between Nellore and Narsapur, south of Ongole, after moving across the west-central Bay of Bengal. It brought sustained wind speeds of 100-110 kmph, with gusts reaching 120 kmph, according to the IMD's forecast before landfall. The storm comes less than a week after Cyclone Arnab affected parts of India's eastern coast. Lakhs evacuated across Andhra and Odisha Deep Dive Andhra Pradesh had stepped up evacuation and disaster management measures ahead of the cyclone's arrival. Around 2,000 people had been evacuated from vulnerable coastal areas, with the administration planning to move approximately 30,000 people to safer locations, as per PTI. Earlier, over 1.6 lakh people were evacuated from five vulnerable districts of Odisha by 6 pm on Monday ahead of cyclone Murasu's landfall, with Ganjam accounting for around 1.5 lakh of those evacuated. At least 1.4 lakh more people are expected to be moved to safer locations as the state steps up its preparations to deal with the cyclone, HT has learnt. Chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu had directed officials to remain on high alert and ensure that rescue, relief and restoration arrangements were in place. The state government had also taken precautionary measures to protect irrigation infrastructure, reservoirs and agricultural land. Around 31,000 electricity poles had been dispatched to facilitate restoration work in case the storm damaged power infrastructure. The administration is now assessing the extent of damage to electricity networks, roads, houses and crops. Heavy rain forecast across Andhra Pradesh, Telangana The IMD had forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall at several places across coastal Andhra Pradesh and Rayalaseema, with extremely heavy rainfall possible at isolated locations. Telangana was also expected to receive heavy rainfall as the weather system moves inland after crossing the coast. Parts of Tamil Nadu, south Odisha and Chhattisgarh were also under a weather alert. The weather department has warned that rainfall activity could continue even after landfall, as the cyclone weakens and moves inland. Flights, trains disrupted due to cyclone Cyclone Murasu disrupted air and rail services ahead of its landfall. At least 30 domestic flights were cancelled on Monday across Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam, Tirupati and Chennai airports because of adverse weather conditions. Railway authorities also cancelled nine trains as a precautionary measure ahead of the cyclone's arrival. Passengers have been advised to check with airlines and railway authorities for updated schedules and service information. Odisha, Tamil Nadu step up relief measures Odisha had moved more than 1.6 lakh people to safer locations as a precaution, with several southern districts placed on alert. Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri were among the districts expected to receive heavy rainfall. Rescue teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF) and fire services were kept ready for emergency operations. Tamil Nadu had also extended assistance to Andhra Pradesh by sending three NDRF teams comprising 90 personnel and electricity department teams with 500 personnel to support rescue and power restoration work. The back-to-back cyclones have raised concerns over further damage to agriculture and infrastructure, particularly in areas still recovering from Cyclone Arnab. Storm surge, fishermen warned against venturing into sea Before landfall, the IMD had warned of a storm surge of around 1 to 1.5 metres above the astronomical tide in low-lying areas of south coastal Andhra Pradesh. The warning covered vulnerable stretches of the coast, including parts of Bapatla, Krishna and Prakasam districts. Fishermen had been advised not to venture into the sea, with rough conditions expected over the west-central Bay of Bengal and along the Andhra Pradesh coast. news.full_article_text: Meghalaya: Paul Lyngdoh returns as minister; Metbah quits cabinet after UDP collapse The development marks a major reversal for the UDP, which won 12 seats in the 2023 assembly elections and emerged as a significant regional force Meghalaya’s United Democratic Party (UDP) president Metbah Lyngdoh lost his cabinet berth following the political upheaval that reduced his party to a one-man outfit. Meanwhile, former party colleague Paul Lyngdoh returned to the Conrad K Sangma government as a minister, this time representing the National People’s Party (NPP). Paul, the West Shillong legislator who left the UDP for the NPP along with two other party colleagues, was sworn in as a cabinet minister by governor CH Vijayashankar at Lok Bhavan on Monday evening. He was allocated the tourism portfolio, which he previously held before being dropped in the September 2025 cabinet reshuffle. His induction follows Metbah’s resignation from the cabinet on October 31, after 11 of the UDP’s 12 legislators left the party, with eight joining the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and three moving to the NPP. Metbah, who held the power, water resources, taxation and textiles portfolios, submitted his resignation to chief minister Conrad K Sangma with immediate effect, saying he could no longer continue as a minister after being left as the party’s sole legislator. “After very thorough and careful consideration, I have taken the decision that I will not be able to continue as Cabinet minister in the MDA government,” he said, adding that his resignation was the first decision taken by the party and that further decisions would follow. The development marks a major reversal for the UDP, which won 12 seats in the 2023 assembly elections and emerged as a significant regional force. The speaker formally recognised the merger of eight legislators with the BJP on October 16, followed by the recognition of the merger of three others with the NPP on October 23. The BJP’s strength consequently rose from two to 10, while the NPP increased its tally from 33 to 36. The UDP was left with Metbah as its sole MLA. The political crisis was building since September, when eight legislators — Lahkmen Rymbui, Pius Marwein, Kyrmen Shylla, Mayralborn Syiem, Matthew Beyondstar Kurbah, Ollan Singh Suin, Balajied Kupar Synrem and Synshar Kupar Roy Lyngdoh Thabah — joined the BJP. They cited assurances on long-pending regional issues, including the inclusion of Khasi and Garo languages in the Constitution’s Eighth Schedule, implementation of the Meghalaya Residents Safety and Security Act, coal mining and the relocation of the Harijan Colony from Them Iew Mawlong. The subsequent departure of Paul, Renikton Lyngdoh Tongkhar and Nujorki Sungoh to the NPP virtually wiped out the UDP’s legislative presence. Metbah had earlier expressed surprise at the mass exodus, questioning why legislators elected on UDP tickets had abandoned the party. He maintained that the organisation continued to exist despite the defections and said it would prepare for the 2028 Assembly elections. Metbah insisted that his resignation was not taken under pressure. “I will never take any decision under pressure because under pressure you will make lots of mistakes,” he said, adding that the party’s Central Executive Committee will decide whether the UDP would continue supporting the MDA government. The issue is expected to be discussed at the party’s November 3 meeting. Paul, meanwhile, said he had neither demanded nor suggested any particular portfolio. He said the chief minister wanted continuity in the Tourism Department and asked him to take charge. “I gladly accepted, considering the challenges that have emerged over the past few days,” he said. He said his immediate priority would be to put the department back on track, consult stakeholders and review tourism projects, while strengthening safety arrangements for visitors and residents. As the UDP struggles to chart a future with its president as its only legislator, one of its former senior leaders returned to the cabinet under the banner of the party that absorbed him. For Metbah, the November 3 meeting could prove crucial in determining the UDP’s next political course, including its position within the ruling MDA coalition. For Paul, the return to office marks a fresh chapter in a political realignment that has fundamentally altered Meghalaya’s regional party landscape.

news.headline: Delhi's smog came from farm fires lit after NASA's satellite passed
news.story_lead: Delhi's smog came from farm fires lit after NASA's satellite passed On two Oct nights with the same weather, Delhi's air was far cleaner. India's weather satellite shows surge in evening crop burning in the 4 days before Nov 1. Smoke from farm fires in Punjab and Haryana drove the sharp rise in Delhi's pollution on Sunday, which pushed the air into the " very poor " range on Monday, an HT analysis of air-quality, weather and satellite data has found.
news.full_article_text: Delhi's smog came from farm fires lit after NASA's satellite passed On two Oct nights with the same weather, Delhi's air was far cleaner. India's weather satellite shows surge in evening crop burning in the 4 days before Nov 1. Smoke from farm fires in Punjab and Haryana drove the sharp rise in Delhi's pollution on Sunday, which pushed the air into the " very poor " range on Monday, an HT analysis of air-quality, weather and satellite data has found. Most of the fires were lit in the evening, after the NASA satellite whose count is the standard measure of stubble burning had passed over the region. Delhi's air quality index, which runs from 0 to 500, rose from 117 on Saturday to 261 on Sunday. By Monday morning the Central Pollution Control Board's (CPCB) hourly reading had crossed 300, the threshold for "very poor" air. Monday's 4pm bulletin put the index at 324, the season's first very poor reading. The last very poor reading this year was on February 11. ALSO READ: GRAP-II pollution curbs imposed in Delhi-NCR as air quality dips further Deep Dive The weather in the run-up was poor, with little wind and a still night. But Delhi had the same weather on October 18 and 28, and the air on those nights was far cleaner. The clearest measure is PM2.5, the fine particles that do the most harm because they reach deep into the lungs. India's limit for PM2.5, averaged over a day, is 60 micrograms per cubic metre of air. On the night of November 1, from 10pm to 6am on Monday, it averaged 194, more than three times that limit. On the October nights it averaged 68 and 127. Same weather, dirtier air HT compared November 1 with every night this season on three measures from the India Meteorological Department's weather balloon and the Safdarjung airfield: how well the afternoon wind cleared the air, how strong the dawn inversion was, and how still the night was. The inversion is a lid of warm air that stops air near the ground from mixing upwards. On October 18 and 28, all three were as bad as on November 1, or worse. Both nights were fully calm, and the lid was at least as strong. Yet the air on the night of November 1 held nearly three times as much PM2.5 as on October 18, and about half as much again as on October 28. Not a rebound from the rain Rain on October 29 and 30 washed the air, and the index fell to 60 on Friday. The index is an average of the past 24 hours, so as those clean hours dropped out of it, the index would have risen anyway. The hourly readings, however, show that by the morning of November 1 the air was about as dirty as on the morning of October 28. The two days diverged after that. The pollution came in by day On a bad morning in Delhi, pollution trapped overnight hangs low over the city. As the sun warms the ground, the air starts to churn, the pollution spreads upward, and readings at street level fall. Pollution from the city's own traffic, trapped overnight, thins out this way. On October 28, PM2.5 fell by nearly two-thirds by mid-afternoon. On October 18, it fell by more than half. On November 1, it did not fall at all: it was slightly higher in the afternoon than in the morning. Readings hold steady only when the air higher up is as dirty as the air at street level, or when dirty air is blowing in. Either way, the extra pollution on November 1 came from outside Delhi. It had begun to show a day earlier. Around midday on October 31, PM2.5 nearly doubled in three hours, the sharpest midday rise this season. It stayed high into Monday morning. The extra pollution was also made up of the finest particles. On the night of November 1, they made up nearly six-tenths of all the particulate matter in the air by weight, against just over four-tenths on the October nights. Smoke is mostly fine; road and construction dust is coarse. The fires NASA's count misses The count most often quoted for stubble burning comes from a NASA satellite that passes over Punjab once a day, at about 1.30pm. Farmers no longer burn at that hour. More than 90% of large fires in Punjab in 2024 and 2025 were lit after 3pm, against 3% in 2021, according to the Stubble Burning Status Report 2025 by iFOREST, a New Delhi research group. HT checked this against geostationary satellites, which stay over the same spot and scan the region through the day. They see in coarser detail than NASA's satellite and pick up only large or intense fires, but they show when the burning happens. Last season, 99% of the fires India's INSAT-3DS satellite spotted in Punjab and Haryana were burning after 3pm. This season, INSAT-3DS saw almost no evening fires from October 15 to 28. Then the count climbed day after day, from 17 on October 29 to 90 on November 1. Because it sees only the bigger fires, far more fields burned than it counted. NASA's count also rose, to 171 on November 1, the season's highest. But through October it did not rise and fall with Delhi's air. On October 18 and 28 it recorded more than 100 fires each day, yet Delhi's afternoons on both days were cleaner than usual for the season. The difference lay in the wind. The air had crossed the fires The winds that carry pollution over long distances, a few hundred metres to a kilometre or two up and known as transport-level winds, blew from the north-west on the afternoons of October 31 and November 1, according to the Safdarjung balloon readings. That is the direction of the fire belt. On October 28 they blew from the south. HT also used wind data from two global weather models to trace where the air reaching Delhi had been over the previous three days. On November 1, it had spent most of that time over Punjab and Haryana, passing over dozens of fires that the satellites had spotted in the day before. On October 28, it came in from the east, away from the fire belt, and passed few fires. On October 18, it crossed Punjab, but before the evening burning had begun, and the city stayed comparatively clean. What the data cannot show HT's analysis cannot measure how much of the November 1 pollution was smoke. The damp air left behind by the rain may also have played a part, because humid air helps some gases turn into fine particles. Humidity was above 90% on the nights of October 31 and November 1, against 76% on October 28. But it was just as humid on October 31 as on November 1, and the afternoon air on November 1 was far dirtier. NASA's count for the season so far is about a quarter lower than last year's for the same dates. Most burning now happens after its satellite has gone, so the lower count says little about whether fewer fields burned. INSAT's count of evening fires was still rising on November 1. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Binayak Dasgupta Binayak Dasgupta is a senior editor at Hindustan Times, New Delhi, where he has worked since 2013.
